screening_decisions.reason: This is an RCT of adults with heart failure (mean age 75). The intervention uses a tablet computer that delivers HF education (information and lifestyle advice per guidelines), which is mHealth-delivered education. The control group received standard information (usual care). Thus, all inclusion criteria (RCT, adults ≥18 with HF, mHealth education, usual care comparator) are satisfied.

Randomized controlled trial (three-group parallel-randomized). Adults (mean age 66.8 years) with heart failure. Intervention is the heartfailurematters.org website, an internet/web-based education programme (mHealth-delivered education) plus an e-health adjusted care pathway, compared to usual HF care. Meets all inclusion criteria.

The study is an RCT (randomized controlled design). It targets adults with heart failure (HF patients). The intervention is a web-based self-care education program, which qualifies as mHealth-delivered education as it is accessible via internet/web-based platforms intended for use on smartphones/tablets/other mobile devices. Although the abstract does not specify the comparator, it likely involves usual HF care, and in the absence of contradicting information, we include. The study is a pilot, but the selection criteria do not exclude feasibility studies.
Conservative inclusion due to unclear education component

The study is an RCT involving adults with HF, but the intervention is not mHealth-delivered education. The intervention consists of nurse-led face-to-face counseling, computer-based education (unspecified whether mobile, likely traditional computer), and written materials. This does not meet the protocol's definition of mHealth-delivered education, which requires mobile/wireless technologies (e.g., smartphone/tablet apps, SMS, social media). Therefore, the study is excluded.

The intervention consists of nurse-led counselling, computer-based education, and written materials. There is no indication that the education component is delivered via mobile/wireless technologies (e.g., smartphone/tablet apps, SMS, social media) as required by the selection criteria. The computer-based education could be desktop-based and does not explicitly meet the mHealth-delivered education definition. Therefore the intervention does not fulfil the inclusion criterion.

The intervention in the SCOOP II trial was a nurse-guided education program, facilitated telephone communication, and scheduled follow-up visits. There is no evidence that the education was delivered through mHealth technologies as defined by the review (mobile and wireless technologies such as internet/web-based programs for smartphones/tablets, apps, SMS, or social media). The telephone communication does not constitute mHealth-delivered education, as it does not utilize modern mobile health technologies for education delivery and does not fit the review’s specification. Therefore, the study does not meet the intervention criterion.

The study is an RCT in adults with HF (criteria met for design and population). However, the intervention is 'video education' added to standard education. The abstract does not specify that the video education was delivered via mobile or wireless technologies (mHealth) such as smartphones, tablets, apps, SMS, or social media, as required by the review protocol. Without evidence of mHealth delivery, the intervention criterion is not met.

The study is a pilot study with only 8 patients, no randomization, and no comparison group. The selection criteria require randomised controlled trials (RCTs). The study design does not meet this criterion, so it is excluded.

The study is not a randomised controlled trial; it is a descriptive analysis of the recruitment process for an mHealth trial. The intervention (smartphone app for medication management and communication) is not mHealth-delivered education. The population includes patients with hypertension and dyslipidemia, not exclusively heart failure. Thus it fails study design, intervention, and population criteria.

The intervention is a web-based compliance monitoring device, not an mHealth-delivered education programme. The study does not describe educational content (e.g., web-based education modules, smartphone apps for education, SMS educational messages); it focuses on monitoring medication adherence and self-care behaviors via a device and web-based dashboard. Therefore, it does not meet the intervention criterion.
The study is a proof-of-concept field study using an exploratory inquiry and qualitative methods, not a randomised controlled trial (RCT). Therefore it fails the study design criterion.
The study is a descriptive survey design assessing usability, not a randomised controlled trial. It does not meet the study design criterion (RCT).

The intervention is a multi-component collaborative care disease management program including telemonitoring and depression treatment, not specifically mHealth-delivered education as required. The protocol does not describe an mHealth education intervention (e.g., mobile apps, SMS, web-based education programs) but rather a broader care model.

The study tests a collaborative care PCDM intervention that includes multidisciplinary team, home telemonitoring, self-management support, and depression treatment, but not an mHealth-delivered education program as required by the selection criteria. The abstract does not describe education delivery via mobile technologies.

The CASA trial is an RCT of a collaborative care model that uses phone-based symptom management and psychosocial support, not an mHealth-delivered education program. The intervention does not involve mobile/wireless technologies to deliver health education (e.g., apps, SMS, web-based platforms) as required by the protocol. Therefore, it fails the intervention criterion.

The study is a six-month randomized field experiment (RCT) comparing a technology-enhanced practice model including a web-based home care resource (HeartCareII) to usual care. The intervention is a web-based education/resource platform, which qualifies as mHealth-delivered education. The population is home care patients; although the abstract does not explicitly state heart failure diagnosis, the name 'HeartCareII' strongly suggests cardiac patients, possibly heart failure. Following conservative screening, this study is included for full-text review to verify eligibility.

The study is an RCT in adults with chronic heart failure, but the intervention is motivational interviewing delivered primarily through in-person sessions and telephone follow-up, not mHealth-delivered education as defined by the protocol (i.e., internet/web-based programs, apps, SMS, or social media). Telephone follow-up does not meet the definition of mHealth-delivered education.

The study population is Indigenous people with cardiovascular disease or at risk, not specifically heart failure. The study design is an intervention trial with pre/post measures, not a randomised controlled trial. The comparison is not usual heart failure care. Does not meet population, study design, or comparison criteria.

RCT with adult HF patients comparing a mobile phone-based disease management program (which includes self-care education, as evidenced by measured knowledge and self-efficacy outcomes) versus usual care. This aligns with mHealth-delivered education using mobile technology. Despite the broader 'case management' label, the educational component is central, fulfilling the intervention criterion.

The intervention is telehomecare (remote monitoring of clinical indices and nurse intervention), not an mHealth-delivered education programme such as internet/web-based education, apps, SMS messages, or social media. No educational component is described in the abstract.

The study does not appear to be an RCT (mentions repeated measures design, no randomization stated). The intervention is a telehealth system transmitting data over telephone lines, not mHealth-delivered education as defined (smartphone/tablet apps, SMS, social media). Focus is on self-management via confidence, not education. Population is older adults but not explicitly >=18 with HF diagnosis, though likely. Does not meet study design and intervention criteria.

The intervention is a telehealth system (Health Buddy) used for remote monitoring and support after homecare discharge. It does not clearly correspond to an mHealth-delivered education intervention such as a smartphone/tablet app, web-based education programme, SMS, or social media-delivered education. The study lacks a description of an educational curriculum or content delivery via mobile technology; rather, it is a continuous home monitoring system.

RCT with adult HF patients; intervention is internet-based synchronized face-to-face group education sessions (mHealth education). The comparison group received a self-care handout, exercise routine, and Fitbit, which may exceed usual care but could still be considered standard self-care. Given conservative screening, include.

The study employed a quasi-experimental design with a convenience sample (non-randomised), whereas the protocol requires a randomised controlled trial (RCT). Therefore it fails the study design criterion.
Study describes development and feasibility testing of a web-based education program with 12 volunteers. No randomized comparison to usual care; not an RCT.

RCT in adults with HF, but the intervention is an e-mail reminder to the patient's nurse, not mHealth-delivered education directly to patients with heart failure. The protocol requires mHealth education interventions for people with HF (e.g., smartphone apps, SMS, web-based programs), not provider-targeted reminders. Therefore, the intervention does not meet the selection criteria.
Not an RCT: this is a single-arm feasibility study with convenience sampling, no randomization and no control group. Study design explicitly states a larger randomized sample is needed.

The study evaluates a comprehensive telerehabilitation program (telemonitoring and telecoaching) added to standard cardiac rehabilitation, not a specific mHealth-delivered education intervention. It does not mention educational components and compares to standard cardiac rehabilitation rather than usual HF care alone.

The study is a systematic literature review, not a randomised controlled trial (RCT). Additionally, it addresses chronic disease management broadly, not specifically adults with heart failure, and the interventions evaluated are home-based information and communications technology interventions, which may not align with mHealth-delivered education as defined in the criteria. Therefore, it clearly fails to meet the study design, population, and intervention criteria.

The study tests telemonitoring of medication adherence, an intervention focused on monitoring rather than providing mHealth-delivered education (e.g., no educational content via smartphone/tablet app, SMS, or social media). Moreover, the comparator was passive adherence monitoring, not usual heart failure care as required.

The study includes a mixed population of HF and COPD patients without separate HF results, thus not meeting the population criterion. The intervention is a multifaceted telehealth program, not specifically mHealth-delivered education (e.g., apps, SMS, web-based). The comparison group was usual care plus education, not usual HF care alone. Therefore, it fails intervention, population, and comparison criteria.

The intervention is a medication reminder app, not an mHealth-delivered education programme as specified (no educational content provided). Additionally, the study lacks a usual HF care comparison arm. Thus, it fails both intervention and comparison criteria.

The study is an RCT enrolling adults with HF, but the intervention is a remote medication monitoring system (MedSentry) focused on tracking and reminding medication adherence, not on providing health education. It does not fit the mHealth-delivered education criteria defined by the review (e.g., internet-based education programmes, SMS education, apps for learning). Thus, it fails the intervention criterion.

The study evaluates integrated care services supported by information technology for multiple chronic conditions (COPD, cardiac failure, diabetes), not a trial of mHealth-delivered education specifically for heart failure. The intervention does not constitute an mHealth education programme (e.g., apps, SMS, web-based education) as required by the protocol; rather, it is a broad care delivery model. Using conservative judgment, the study clearly does not meet the intervention criterion.

The abstract describes a trial of behavioral support for smoking reduction among disadvantaged smokers. The population is not adults with heart failure; the intervention is not mHealth-delivered education for HF; the comparator is not usual HF care. Thus, it fails all selection criteria.

The intervention is an Internet-based telemedicine system for frequent surveillance and communication, not an mHealth-delivered education programme as defined by the review (education via apps, SMS, web-based learning). Therefore, it does not meet the intervention criteria.

The study evaluates a web-based telemedicine system for surveillance and communication, not an mHealth-delivered education program. The intervention focuses on monitoring health status and reporting, with no educational content or learning materials described. Therefore, it does not meet the intervention criterion.

The study evaluates a telemonitoring device for medication adherence support, not an mHealth-delivered education programme. The selection criteria specifically require mHealth education interventions (e.g., internet/web-based education, apps, SMS messages, or social media-delivered education). The described intervention lacks an educational component and focuses on adherence monitoring and support, thus failing to meet the intervention criterion.
The study is an overview of systematic reviews, not a randomised controlled trial (RCT). It does not meet the study design criterion.
The study is a meta-analysis and economic model, not a randomized controlled trial. Therefore, it does not meet the study design criterion requiring an RCT.

The study is a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, not itself a randomized controlled trial, thus failing the RCT study design criterion. Furthermore, the intervention evaluated is telemonitoring of cardiac implantable electronic devices, which is not mHealth-delivered education (e.g., internet, apps, SMS) as defined in the protocol. Therefore, it does not meet the inclusion criteria.

The intervention is telemonitoring and ICT-guided disease management, not mHealth-delivered education. There is no educational component (e.g., apps, SMS, social media for education). The comparison is not usual HF care: both arms received an ICT-guided DMS, so no true control of usual care.

The study is a systematic review of controlled clinical studies, not a randomized controlled trial (RCT). The review protocol requires an RCT design; therefore, it does not meet the study design criterion.

The intervention is a clinical decision-support rule-set for medication adjustments, not an mHealth-delivered education program. The protocol explicitly requires mHealth-based education (apps, SMS, web-based education, social media). This study focuses on decision support for medication management, which does not meet the educational intervention criterion.

The study is not a randomised controlled trial (RCT); it is a retrospective analysis of a telephonic health coaching programme with no comparison group. Furthermore, the intervention (telephonic health coaching) does not meet the definition of mHealth-delivered education (internet/web-based apps, SMS, social media). The population is a mixed high-risk group, not exclusively adults with heart failure.

Study participants are sedentary young adults without a diagnosis of heart failure; the trial focuses on heart disease risk prevention in healthy individuals, not mHealth-delivered education for heart failure patients versus usual HF care.

The study evaluates mHealth equipment for remote monitoring (connected to a 24-hour call center or digital home equipment) in older adults with HF. It does not deliver any educational intervention such as internet/web-based education programmes, SMS messages, or social media-delivered education. The intervention is focused on monitoring and self-management tools, not mHealth-delivered education, thus it fails the intervention criterion.

Not an RCT: the abstract describes a qualitative sub-study (face-to-face interviews, qualitative content analysis) of a telehealth feasibility trial, with no mention of randomization or controlled comparison. The selection criteria require randomized controlled trials; therefore this study is excluded.
Population: Recruited from coronary heart disease registries, not specifically heart failure. The study does not meet the population criterion (adults with diagnosis of heart failure).

The study is an RCT involving adults with heart failure, but the intervention is systematic nurse/pharmacist-led education using a Kodak Photo-CD Portfolio technique, which is a face-to-face, traditional education method, not mHealth-delivered education (internet, web-based, smartphones, tablets, apps, SMS, social media). Therefore, it does not meet the intervention criterion.

The intervention is an interactive CD-ROM program, which is not a mobile or wireless technology (mHealth). It does not involve internet/web-based platforms, smartphone/tablet apps, SMS, or social media. Therefore, the study does not meet the intervention criterion.
The study uses a quasi-experimental design, not a randomised controlled trial (RCT) as required by the review protocol.
Not a randomised controlled trial; it is a single-arm pilot/proof-of-concept study with no comparison group. The protocol requires an RCT design.

Study design is not a RCT (feasibility/proof-of-concept study without randomization). Intervention is internet-based cognitive behavior therapy, which is not mHealth-delivered education as defined. Therefore, fails both study design and intervention criteria.

The study does not compare mHealth education to usual HF care; both arms are web-based interventions (ICBT vs discussion forum). Additionally, the intervention is cognitive behavioral therapy, not an mHealth-delivered education program for self-care.

The study is an RCT of remote monitoring and fluid monitoring in HF patients with implanted devices. The intervention involves device-based remote monitoring (RM) and fluid monitoring (FM), which is a monitoring strategy, not an mHealth-delivered education programme (e.g., no internet-based education, apps for learning, SMS education, or social media education). Therefore, it does not meet the intervention criterion of mHealth-delivered education.

The study is an RCT in adults with heart failure, but the intervention is home telemonitoring, which involves remote monitoring of physiological parameters and health status, not mHealth-delivered education as defined by the protocol (e.g., educational programmes via smartphone apps, SMS, or social media). Telemonitoring is a monitoring technology rather than an educational intervention, so it does not meet the intervention criterion.

The study is an RCT of a multidisciplinary disease management programme (MDP) for heart failure, but the intervention does not involve mHealth-delivered education (no mention of mobile/wireless technology, web-based education, apps, SMS, or social media). Therefore, it does not meet the intervention criterion.

The intervention is motivational interviewing (MI) delivered via home and phone-based sessions, not an mHealth-delivered education programme (e.g., internet/web-based education, apps, SMS, social media). MI is a behavioral counseling approach, not an educational intervention using mobile or wireless technologies as defined. Thus, it does not meet the intervention criterion.

The intervention is a nurse-led motivational interviewing program delivered via home visit and telephone calls, which does not meet the definition of mHealth-delivered education (e.g., internet/web-based programs, smartphone apps, SMS, or social media). Therefore, it fails the intervention criterion.

The study is not an RCT; it is a cost-effectiveness analysis that synthesises data from 13 existing RCTs using a decision model. This fails the study design criterion (must be a randomised controlled trial). Additionally, the intervention evaluated is implantable cardiac devices (ICD, CRT-P, CRT-D), not mHealth-delivered education. Therefore, the study clearly does not meet the selection criteria.

Study design is retrospective cohort, not RCT. Population is ICD recipients, not specifically diagnosed heart failure patients. Intervention is remote monitoring (device data transmission), not mHealth-delivered education (e.g., apps, SMS, web-based patient education). Thus fails multiple inclusion criteria (design, population, intervention).

The study population consists of home health nurses, not adults with heart failure. The intervention targets nurses to change clinical practice, not mHealth-delivered education for heart failure patients. Therefore, it does not meet the population criterion of adults with HF.

The study compares a tailored tele‑monitoring intervention (delivered via telephone) with usual care. Although the population (adults with heart failure) and study design (RCT) match the criteria, the intervention is not mHealth‑delivered education. The review requires specifically internet/web‑based education programmes, smartphone/tablet apps, SMS‑based education, or social media‑delivered education. Tele‑monitoring via telephone, as described in the abstract, focuses on remote monitoring rather than educational content delivery. Therefore, the study does not meet the intervention criterion.

The study is a qualitative descriptive study involving semi-structured email interviews with practice nurses about their perceptions of a telehealth service for COPD and heart failure patients. It is not a randomised controlled trial (RCT) and does not evaluate an mHealth-delivered education intervention for heart failure patients compared to usual HF care. Therefore, it does not meet the study design or intervention criteria.

The intervention is a combined health coaching telephone calls and telemonitoring (remote patient monitoring) after discharge, not mHealth-delivered education. The review requires mHealth-based education such as internet/web-based education programs for smartphones/tablets, apps, SMS, or social media-delivered education. This study focuses on monitoring vital signs and coaching calls, not delivering educational content via mobile/wireless technologies.

This study is a systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs, not a primary randomised controlled trial itself. The review protocol requires primary RCTs. Therefore, it does not meet the study design criterion.

The study is a review article, not a randomised controlled trial. It does not evaluate an mHealth-delivered education intervention but rather discusses monitoring devices. Therefore, it does not meet the selection criteria of being an RCT comparing mHealth-delivered education versus usual HF care.

Population not exclusive to heart failure: includes mixed chronic diseases (diabetes, CAD, CHF). Intervention is telephone coaching, not a specified mHealth education mode (apps, SMS, web-based). Does not meet population or intervention criteria.

RCT and HF population met. However, the intervention is telemonitoring of vital parameters and telephone support, not mHealth-delivered education. The protocol requires education delivered via mobile/wireless technologies (apps, SMS, web-based programmes). No educational component is described; it is a monitoring/management tool. Therefore, does not meet intervention criteria.

The intervention is remote patient monitoring (RPM) with live nursing visits and video-based nursing visits. This is a telehealth monitoring service, not an mHealth-delivered education programme (e.g., internet/web-based education, SMS, or social media-delivered education). The study does not meet the intervention criterion.

The study is a qualitative focus group study using a community-based participatory research approach to adapt a telemonitoring intervention, not a randomised controlled trial. The abstract describes formative work and does not report results from an RCT comparing mHealth education to usual care. Therefore, it fails the study design criterion.

The study is an RCT involving adults with HF, and the intervention (mHealth+CP) includes mHealth education elements (automated calls, email summaries). However, the comparison group (standard mHealth) is also an active mHealth intervention delivering automated self-care support calls, not usual HF care. The review protocol requires comparison to usual HF care. Therefore, the study does not meet the selection criteria.

The study is a protocol for a randomized trial, not an actual completed RCT reporting outcomes. The selection criteria specify that studies must be 'conducted as a randomised controlled trial (RCT)', implying a completed study with results. Additionally, the intervention is an IVR-based care transition monitoring system (E-Coach) which does not qualify as mHealth-delivered education as defined in the criteria (internet/web-based education programmes for smartphones/tablets, SMS messages, or social media). The focus is on monitoring and nurse alerts, not patient education.

The study evaluates a care transition support program (E-Coach) consisting of nurse support, IVR calls, and follow-up, which is not an mHealth-delivered education intervention (e.g., internet/web-based education, apps, SMS, social media) as specified in the protocol. The intervention does not match the required intervention criterion.

The study is an RCT in adults with heart failure. The intervention is a web-based online medical record with an educational guide, which constitutes an mHealth-delivered education programme. The comparison is usual care. Despite the intervention not being solely an education programme, its educational component meets the criteria. Therefore, included.

The study enrolls adults based on family history risk, not those with a diagnosis of heart failure. The intervention is a tailored preventive messages tool for multiple diseases, not mHealth-delivered education for heart failure self-management. The comparison is an age/sex-specific health message, not usual heart failure care. Thus it fails population, intervention, and comparison criteria.

The study abstract describes an analysis of time-weighted mean HbA1c and mortality in patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic heart failure, with no mention of an mHealth education intervention, randomization, or comparison to usual care. It does not meet the inclusion criteria for study design (RCT), intervention (mHealth education), or comparison.
Study design is qualitative focus group, not a randomised controlled trial (RCT). Therefore, it clearly does not meet the inclusion criteria.

This study is a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with patients and clinicians, not a randomised controlled trial. Therefore it does not meet the study design criterion of the review protocol.

The intervention is mobile phone-based telemonitoring (daily readings, symptom tracking, alerts), not an mHealth-delivered education programme as defined in the criteria (e.g., educational modules, apps for learning). No dedicated educational component is described.

The intervention is a smartphone-based telemonitoring system for clinical decision support, not an mHealth-delivered education program. The study does not involve any form of education delivery via mobile technology (such as educational apps, SMS, or social media). Therefore, it does not meet the intervention criteria.
Intervention is telephone-based, not mHealth (internet/web, apps, SMS, social media). Does not meet intervention criterion.

The study evaluates a computer-based educational programme, not mHealth-delivered education. mHealth requires mobile and wireless technologies (e.g., smartphone/tablet apps, SMS, social media), which are absent from the intervention description. Therefore, it does not satisfy the intervention criterion.

Excluded: Intervention does not meet the mHealth-delivered education criterion. The study evaluates remote monitoring of cardiac implantable electronic devices for follow-up and device management, not an educational program delivered via mobile/wireless technologies (e.g., smartphone apps, SMS, social media) to educate heart failure patients. Therefore, it is outside the scope of this review.

The study evaluates motivational interviewing, not mHealth-delivered education. The abstract makes no mention of internet/web-based delivery, smartphone/tablet apps, SMS, or social media. The intervention does not meet the specified mHealth education criterion.

The study is a pilot RCT of home telemonitoring for patients with congestive heart failure and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The intervention is remote monitoring of physiological parameters, not mHealth-delivered education. No educational component (e.g., app-based learning, SMS education, web-based modules) is mentioned. Additionally, the study population includes both heart failure and COPD patients, so it does not exclusively target adults with HF; the HF subgroup is not separately reported. Therefore, it does not meet the intervention or population criteria.

The intervention is a mailed DVD and booklet, which is not mHealth-delivered education (mobile/wireless technologies such as smartphone/tablet apps, SMS, web-based). Therefore, it does not meet the intervention criterion of the review.

The study evaluates telemonitoring and telecare using a handheld PDA for daily clinical monitoring and communication, which is not an mHealth-delivered education programme as defined in the review. The intervention lacks educational content; it is a monitoring system. Therefore, it does not meet the inclusion criteria for mHealth-delivered education.
Study design is not an RCT; it is a cross-sectional survey and quality assessment of existing consumer information materials. No mHealth intervention is tested against usual HF care.
The study is described as a 'prospective study' and used a retrospectively matched control group, with no mention of random allocation. This does not meet the RCT design criterion.
Retrospective study design; not a randomised controlled trial (RCT). The review requires RCTs only.

The study is a retrospective case-matched chart review, not an RCT (excluded by design). The intervention is remote monitoring services, not mHealth-delivered education as defined (mobile apps, SMS, web-based education platforms for heart failure self-care). No relevant comparison of mHealth education to usual care.

The study is a feasibility study enrolling 30 healthy volunteers, not an RCT. It does not meet the population criterion (adults with HF) nor the study design (RCT). The intervention is telemonitoring (remote data transmission) rather than mHealth-delivered education. Therefore, it is clearly excluded.

The abstract describes a longitudinal study of psychological distress in Bosnian war survivors, not a randomised controlled trial of mHealth-delivered education in adults with heart failure. The population, intervention, and study design do not match any inclusion criteria.

The study is a methodological taxonomy development, not a randomised controlled trial. It does not involve adults with heart failure, nor does it test an mHealth education intervention versus usual care. Therefore, it fails all inclusion criteria (study design, population, intervention, and comparison).

This is a retrospective registry analysis (GWTG-HF), not a randomised controlled trial. It does not evaluate any mHealth-delivered education intervention; it only describes characteristics and outcomes of nonadherent HF patients. Therefore it fails both the study design (RCT required) and the intervention criteria.

The intervention is a nurse-coordinated disease management program with telephone-based monitoring and education, not an mHealth-delivered education intervention as specified (internet/web-based education programmes for smartphones/tablets, apps, SMS messages, social media). Therefore, it does not meet the intervention criteria.

The study is not a randomized controlled trial (RCT), but a descriptive article about a grading system for evidence quality and strength of recommendations in clinical guidelines. It does not include adults with heart failure, nor does it compare an mHealth-delivered education intervention (e.g., internet/web-based programmes, apps, SMS, social media) to usual HF care. No element of the study meets the selection criteria.

The intervention uses telephone-based counseling and education, which does not clearly map to the protocol-defined mHealth modalities (internet/web-based apps, SMS, social media). Moreover, the comparator is a brief one-hour education session, not usual HF care as required.
The abstract describes epidemiology and risk factors of heart failure, without any mention of an RCT or mHealth-delivered education intervention; it does not meet the selection criteria.

This is a narrative review article, not a randomised controlled trial. It does not evaluate an mHealth-delivered education intervention compared to usual heart failure care. Therefore, it fails to meet the study design and intervention criteria.

Study is an epidemiological review of HFpEF, not a randomised controlled trial. It does not evaluate any mHealth-delivered education intervention compared to usual HF care, therefore does not meet any of the inclusion criteria (study design, intervention, comparison) and should be excluded.

Study design is not an RCT; it is a secondary analysis of a cross-sectional, observational study. The intervention is absent: the study examines mediating pathways (self-care confidence) between social support and adherence, not an mHealth-delivered education intervention. Thus it fails both design and intervention criteria.
The study population consists of adults with type 2 diabetes, not heart failure as required by the selection criteria. Therefore, it does not meet the population criterion.

The study is a prospective cohort study, not a randomised controlled trial. It does not involve any mHealth-delivered education intervention (e.g., apps, SMS, web-based education). It examines quality of life as a predictor of mortality in HF patients, with no comparison to usual HF care in an experimental design.

The study is a narrative literature review, not a randomised controlled trial. It therefore fails the study design criterion. Furthermore, it does not evaluate an mHealth-delivered education intervention; it reviews factors influencing self-care. Both the design and the absence of the intervention warrant exclusion with high confidence.

The study population is newly diagnosed female patients with early stage breast cancer, not adults with a diagnosis of heart failure. The intervention is an entertainment-based decision aid for breast cancer surgery, not mHealth-delivered education for heart failure. The population and intervention do not meet the review's selection criteria.

The study is not a randomized controlled trial (RCT); it is an individual patient data meta-analysis of self-management interventions. Additionally, the intervention assessed is not specifically mHealth-delivered education (internet/web-based, apps, SMS, social media) as required by the protocol. Does not meet design or intervention criteria.

The study is a meta-analysis examining the association between drug/device-induced ventricular remodeling changes and mortality in heart failure patients. It does not evaluate any mHealth-delivered education intervention (internet/web, apps, SMS, social media). Therefore, it fails the intervention criterion. Furthermore, the study design is a meta-analysis of RCTs, not a primary RCT. Clearly EXCLUDE with high confidence.

The study is a literature review, not a randomised controlled trial (RCT). It focuses on telemedicine remote monitoring for patient satisfaction, not an mHealth-delivered education intervention (e.g., internet/web-based education, apps, SMS). Therefore it fails the study design and intervention criteria.

Population: The study enrolled adults (mean age ~62 years) with chronic heart failure and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), so the adult HF population criterion is clearly met. Study design: This is a randomised, double-blind, active-controlled trial (ATMOSPHERE) with random assignment of 7016 participants, thus satisfying the RCT criterion. Intervention: The trial compares aliskiren (direct renin inhibitor) alone, aliskiren plus enalapril, and enalapril alone. These are pharmacological therapies, not mHealth-delivered education. There is no mobile or wireless technology component, no smartphone/tablet app, no SMS, no social media-based education. The intervention is entirely drug-based. Therefore, it does not meet the mHealth education criterion. Comparison: The reference arm is enalapril alone, which is an ACE inhibitor standard therapy for HFrEF, not 'usual HF care' as defined by the review (which expects standard care without the mHealth education component). The trial compares different drug regimens, not mHealth education versus usual care. Overall, despite meeting population and study design, the intervention and comparison are completely outside the scope of this review. The study tests pharmacotherapy, not mHealth education, and thus must be excluded. There is no uncertainty: EXCLUDE with high confidence.

The study is not a randomised controlled trial; it describes development of a taxonomy for disease management based on literature review and qualitative methods, not a trial comparing mHealth-delivered education versus usual HF care. Does not meet any design or intervention criteria.
The study is a systematic review of RCTs, not a primary randomised controlled trial. Therefore, it does not meet the criterion requiring an RCT study design.

Study is a meta-analysis, not a randomised controlled trial; population is not specifically heart failure patients (structural heart disease with VT); intervention is catheter ablation, not mHealth-delivered education; comparison is medical therapy, not usual HF care.

The study is a systematic review, not a randomised controlled trial (RCT), so it fails the study design criterion. Additionally, the population is not specifically heart failure patients and the intervention is not mHealth-delivered education for HF.

This is an observational cohort study, not a randomised controlled trial, and it does not evaluate any mHealth-delivered education intervention; it only examines the association between numeracy/health literacy and 30-day recidivism in acute heart failure. STUDY TITLE:
Primary care providers' physical activity counseling and referral practices and barriers for cardiovascular disease prevention

STUDY ABSTRACT:
The US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends offering or referring adults who are overweight or obese and have additional cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factors to intensive behavioral counseling interventions to promote a healthful diet and physical activity for CVD prevention. This study determined the proportion of primary care providers (PCPs) who discussed physical activity with most of their at-risk patients and referred them to intensive behavioral counseling, and reported barriers to counseling. Our analyses used data from DocStyles 2015, a Web-based panel survey of 1251 PCPs. Overall, 58.6% of PCPs discussed physical activity with most of their at-risk patients. Among these PCPs, the prevalence of components offered ranged from 98.5% encouraging increased physical activity to 13.9% referring to intensive behavioral counseling. Overall, only 8.1% both discussed physical activity with most at-risk patients and referred to intensive behavioral counseling. Barriers related to PCPs' attitudes and beliefs about counseling (e.g., counseling is not effective) were significantly associated with both discussing physical activity with most at-risk patients and referring them to intensive behavioral counseling (adjusted odds ratio, 1.92; 95% confidence interval, 1.15-3.20). System-level barriers (e.g., referral services not available) were not. Just over half of PCPs discussed physical activity with most of their at-risk patients, and few both discussed physical activity and referred patients to intensive behavioral counseling. Overcoming barriers related to attitudes and beliefs about physical activity counseling could help improve low levels of counseling and referrals to intensive behavioral counseling for CVD prevention.

STUDY TITLE:
A systematic review of mhealth-based heart failure interventions

STUDY ABSTRACT:
BackgroundThe popularity of mobile phones and similar mobile devices makes it an ideal medium for delivering interventions. This is especially true with heart failure (HF) interventions, in which mHealth-based HF interventions are rapidly replacing their telephone-based predecessors.PurposeThis systematic review examined the impact of mHealth-based HF management interventions on HF outcomes. The specific aims of the systematic review are to:(1) describe current mHealth-based HF interventions and (2) discuss the impact of these interventions on HF outcomes.MethodsPubMed, CINAHL Plus, Embase, PsycINFO, and Scopus were systematically searched for randomized controlled trials or quasi-experimental studies that tested mHealth interventions in people with HF using the terms Heart Failure, Mobile Health, mHealth, Telemedicine, Text Messaging, Texting, Short Message Service, Mobile Applications, and Mobile Apps.ConclusionsTen articles, representing nine studies, were included in this review. Majority of the studies utilized mobile health technology as part of a HF monitoring system, which typically included a blood pressure measuring device, weighing scale, and an ECG recorder. The impact of the mHealth interventions on all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, HF-related hospitalizations, length of stay, NYHA functional class, LVEF, quality of life, and self-care were inconsistent at best.ImplicationsFurther research is needed to conclusively determine the impact of mHealth interventions on HF outcomes. The limitations of the current studies (eg inadequate sample size, quasi-experimental design, use of older mobile phone models, etc.) should be taken into account when designing future studies.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
